sentences.text: It.
Good morning.
Good morning.
Morning, everyone.
Hi, Andy.
Hey, Andy.
I saw your daughter's book club photograph.
Oh, yeah, the.
What was she called?
Luna.
Love, Love Joy or something.
Obviously very well.
Yeah, very cute.
Yeah.
How are you doing?
You good, Brian?
Yes, all good.
It's all happening at the moment.
It seems to be a lot of interest going on with acquisitions and consolidations.
It seems to be things, things are hotting up, which is a very good sign, obviously.
Yeah, it is, obviously.
We work on both buying the sell side as well, so we're doing a lot of buy side work in the US at the moment.
Yes, all definitely hotting up, which is great.
Hoping that Trump's trade war doesn't derail everything again.
I, I think he did too much too quick.
The rumblings are that Elon is going to be kicked out and.
Oh, that go with the glasses.
He kicks and I'm scared is going to resign.
The Nasdaq went down 4% yesterday.
Tesla's down 44.
I'm watching it.
Tickers.
It's, it's.
And it just makes everybody nervous, especially around marketing services.
So just.

Yeah, it's a pain because everybody was looking forward to Trump getting in because it was good for business and so there had been a little bit of a sort of slowdown while they waited, but he just come in with a, with an ax and it's, it's making everybody nervous again.
He's going to flip, he's going to blame everybody else, he's going to take the people out.
It was all their faults and then do whatever is popular.
How are you doing, Chris?
Good, I'm very well, thank you.
Yes, yeah, all good.
Just busy as well, I suppose.
We've got just enormous amounts going on, which is obviously great.
But, yeah, keeps my day nice and full.
Good.
So it's good to have a nice full day.
You know, I was sharing the query click link with one of our team the other day and I think I put a triple E in instead of A, an E or a double E.
So it's query click like.
Right.
And then some gay website came up.
I think when we launched all the.
Rankings, they used to have all the rankings and we've.
We've dominated them in the 16 years since.
It must be Queer Click.
I.
I guess is their website, but I started sharing this Queer Click website with everybody who's got an ah la.
Sorry about that.
Just having some technicals there.
How are you doing?
Good in yourself?
Yeah, I'm good, thank you.
Sorry, I was just seeing.
Do people call you LA or Leanne.
Yeah, LA.
Leanne.
And another Lindsay.
So brilliant, good name.
Thank you.
So I think this is.
Yeah, we shared some of the details.
I think broadly we understand Capital A is working.
I thought it'd be good just to get everybody together and just have a chat about.
Yeah, here directly from yourself, Andy, just how you work.
Give Chris and LA a chance to ask any questions that they might have before we move to a formal.
Yeah, formal process.
We've got a board meeting on Monday to seek approval, to request approval but just want to get this in beforehand so everybody is aligned.
So Andy, over to you.
Yeah, good stuff.
Okay, so we are a capital A group.
So Capital A is an M and A advisor.
We just work in marketing services.

So all of our clients are involved in either the buying and selling usually of marketing agencies, but everything around that as well, including a lot of measurements and tech and media stuff, but it's all marketing.
Our sell side platform is Agencies Co, so it's a free to list site but we work as an M and A team to sort of make sure that we can bring deals through the process start to finish.
But we use agencies for reach as well, which is really good.
We've got 20,000 subscribers to our mailing list so it's got good reach.

And on the buy side we also work with other agency groups that are in the process of doing roll ups, mergers and we work with private equity as well and sometimes the private equity platform acquisitions helping them to do more bolt ons and just build as they go.
So we've got good visibility on both sides of the table in both buy and sell side.
Probably about 95% of our work is US based, not really intentionally but just the majority of the buyers tend to be from the US and yeah, there's just more of them, more agencies out there.
So we do obviously work in the UK as well.
We're based in the uk.
Yeah, yeah, so that's us I guess the way our process works.
So I did talk through this last time.
I guess the benefit of the newbies so we have kind of like three sort of layers that it works and it works best for different types of scenarios.
So with agencies co, like I said, it's absolutely free to list.
So if somebody wants to list their agency they would have to prepare all of their own materials.
But our MA team is there to swoop in as soon as we have a buyer on the hook.
We're, we run the entire process basically and we tend to do okay with that.
We have had like 45 signed MBAs within 24 hours.
It can be quite an effective way to go, particularly if somebody is not really committed to a time frame and just wants to sort of test the waters and then to prepare all the materials.
So we do have sort of a setup, this sort of suck it and see approach.
So we create the valuation and do the research and make sure that we've got a good valuation for any business that wants to sell.
It does give us and the buyers confidence that, you know, we've gone out into the market and looked for very similar companies that have previously sold recently.
So that process is just 5,000 to the valuation as well as the marketing materials, which just means you don't have to do anything to list on agencies because we provide all of that for you.
And then there's a very in depth process which is more aligned for our clients who kind of just want to get out of the business or they want, want to sell off an agency which is a six month approach.
Sometimes it runs a little bit longer, but we're, we're shooting for a six month process where my team are working on that every single day for at least six months.
And that involves the same process pretty much of putting together the initial valuation and marketing materials and listing on our agency's platform.
But where the difference comes in is that we're also creating a bespoke list of potential buyers.
So we're going out, our analysts will go out into the market and look for every single lead that you can find of the type of agency buyers for that particular type of agency.
And it's a constant process where we're obviously marketing the opportunity to those potential buyers.
We're screening them if we don't know them and make sure there's no tie kicks and time wasters involved in the process.
But it also goes out to our agencies network as well.
We've got 130,000 agencies in our CRM, so we're pretty effective at finding good buyers.
But also we're constantly working on bringing new leads into that process as well.
So it isn't just we send it out to our own mailing list and give up.
It's a constant process of researching and trying to bring new buyers into the process.
And usually over the first two or three months that's lots of meet and greets, see if there's chemistry with the buy side and the sell side.
And if there is, obviously they then start, start to make financial requests and we manage that whole process start to finish.
The idea being that we get to about the four month point and we will have an offer on the table and then leverage the other buyers in the process that have shown an interest, get offers too.

So the best scenario is to have two or three offers on the table at the same time, which we can then leverage to get the best offer with the sort of best buyer, the one that aligns the best culturally.
And then it's usually at least 30 days after the yellow ice is signed to do due diligence and get the contracts done.
And actually with small agencies around the size of this revenue at 1.2 million, that kind of usually is enough.
Sometimes that can run for 60 days.
But all in, you're looking at around a six month process start to finish.
And Andy, in terms of the, the.
Extra work that's involved in that sort of third, third approach, what's the difference you see in EBITDA valuations from taking that approach compared to, you know, just a listing, for example?
So I would say, I mean, there's no real analysis that I've done with that.
So I would just kind of be just more of a sort of process that's run.
Is that because we are getting two to three buyers intentionally at the same time that you're able to push the valuation up.

And so for instance, we've had a situation where we had a client that was happy to sell for sort of 5 or 6 million and we ended up being able to get 13.5 million for the company because we had several large agency groups involved.
And so we were able to get the best offer.
They knew that there was pressure to get a good offer in.
It does work, but I've not done like an, you know, a sort of in depth analysis.

What you need to do is create that sort of contention in the process so that one buyer knows that there are other buyers and that there is, you know, if there's a really good fit, then they're under pressure to put the best offer on the table.
Yeah, of course, you're creating market.
Okay.
Yeah.
And in terms of that listing, you know, how does that work with keeping confidentiality about the agency under discussion?
How do you manage all that?
Yeah, of course.
So I mean, it's completely anonymous, the listing.
We intentionally make sure that we're not using any content from websites that's easy to track down.
So really we're sharing more what we call a teaser.
And that's the teaser sits obviously on agencies as a listing, but also we send that out to target buyers as well.
Nobody knows who the seller is.
And we request for NDAs to be signed if they want to take the next step, which is to get the IM or the CIM or SIN.
And so those NDAs come back and then we present them to you.
So we'll say such a company is interested in viewing the im, are you happy for us to share it?
Obviously, I mean, at the moment we're sharing, we're working with a shopper, media company, software company, which is a very small market, so everybody knows each other.
So in this situation in particular, we've not been able to share to everybody because there's a lot of direct competition in the market.
I would say with what you guys are doing, it's probably less worrisome to share because it's quite an open sort of field.
But there's a lot of agencies in there.
But still the process is exactly the same.
We get to sign the NDAs.
That goes to you first for approval, and then we share the sin.
And, you know, that is where we reveal what the opportunity is.
And they can, obviously, I mean, a lot of buyers actually make the decision just based on what the website looks like.
So I would say 9 out of 10 buyers going forward are just going to check the website, have a good read around, as well as check the financials.
And, you know.

And in terms of this, this deal in particular, you know, clearly I'm the, I'm the founder part of this is about establishing a buyer who wants to take, you know, ownership of that because I have the software component that I need to invest a lot of my time in.
So how do you see the, you know, the lack of the.
Of founder as part of that purchase affecting your process or pricing?
What's your experience there, Andrew?
Yeah, so it doesn't necessarily affect the pricing.
Are you intending to just leave on day one, Chris?
I have some flexibility.
Clearly, it's important to make sure that we're maximizing value, but the intent here is that longer term, my time's invested elsewhere.
Yes, it does.
I mean, generally speaking, it does affect pricing, but it doesn't have to.
It doesn't have to affect it drastically.
So to give you an example, we sold a company that was based in Austin, Texas, fairly recently, and we had a situation where the founder and the CFO were creating the software business on the side.
Their intention was to step away from the business as soon as possible.
We went out to the market with that story.
These guys don't want to stay.
The agency pretty much run itself, but they've got another business and they're focused on growing that.
We got numerous offers but the best one that suited was one that offered a 12 month earn out.
The structure of the deal was what we would typically see for a three year earn out.
But it was hit these targets in 12 months and we'll give you all the cash, you can walk away.
They actually hit the targets in nine months and walked away within nine months.
And so the major point being Chris, that we went to the market with that intention and we would do in this scenario too, we would be like, look, query click is up for sale.
Chris wants to get out as soon as possible and then see what the offers are and then what we can negotiate.
I would say nine out of 10 times we're just going to get a good offer that is based on you working at some kind of condo period.
In agencies it is typically three years.
But like I say we can, we can get the story right and we can negotiate what that looks like.

And if you are available for a 6 to 12 month earnout, I'd say that it is totally doable in terms of affecting the price of something like QueryClick or any agency really it is about the next level of management that's there and whether the system's in place.
I would say given that you are on a 60% profit margin that there probably isn't any management in place.

And so whether the answer is to try, try and sort of make that structure look like there is a kind of COO type person or operations person that could run the day to day very easily or that there were systems in place and actually it's all there.
Somebody just showing the ropes.
Yeah, yeah.
I mean there's some solid, there's some solid structures there.
Yeah.
In which case it shouldn't affect too much.
And like I say, it's just really going to market being extremely clear.

And it could be that if this is like a very, very similar to a SASS play, but if somebody was looking at acquiring something that was a SaaS like business with a 60% margin and then that could be very attractive as well.
So yeah, okay, those are my questions, L.A.
do you have any.
It was really around the systems and the burnout.
That was going to be my question.
I think also as well.
If this is within a sort of holding company structure, I think a lot of buyers, particularly if it was another group, would understand that you're just, you know, rolling this business back out.
So they wouldn't expect a long earn out, they would just see how they could take control of the business and move it into a, into that group.
Andy, what kind of financials do you need?
Do we need to give you three years P and L?
What's.
What do you need for this stage?
Yeah, so three years P, L and the current management accounts or just even just what the current budget is for the year and the forecast.
We do tend to get requests for forecast as well.
So just bear in mind you have to put something together but it's not really based on anything that you can put your name to.
But I would say just don't be too ambitious to try and swing the needle.
You just kind of have to put on sort of 5% growth or something that is completely doable without you getting caught up in a negotiation further down the line.
No differently.
Valuation based on EBITDA or on top end revenue.
So if the buyer is marketing agency, you really want to expect a valuation based on EBITDA.
SaaS businesses do, I don't know 100% whether this is a full SaaS business or not, but they obviously do get valued on revenue multiples.
But at the smaller end of the scale as well they don't tend to be huge multiples even of revenue.
But marketing agencies, they do acquire based on EBITDA multiples.
So I'd say that's the easiest way to go to market if we're expecting a marketing agency to buy it.
And their multiples are never massive.
They do pay much bigger multiples for tech enabled businesses.
So we don't have to be really pessimistic about the valuation either.
But it will most likely still be based on a multiple of ebitda.
And do you have an indication of the sort of what the range is for the EBITDA multiples or business size?
Yeah.
So let me just.
So smaller businesses this end of the market, the multiples generally speaking are kind of between four to six.
That kind of is the sort of standard range for marketing services businesses.
If there's a tech enablement in there, they certainly do go up at the smaller end of the market.
It's never going to be like hair raising multiples.
But equally you can expect some kind of uplift if there is, you know, lots of systems and it's a SAS or SAS like play.
So I would say possibly over six but we really would have to sort of have a good deep dive into the market and see what we can see that's current.
I hate to over promise and get people's expectations too high.
So I would say it could be at the top end of 4 to 6, it could be a bit over that, but I wouldn't expect it to be like a 10x necessarily.
And you've shared the details of how you work and percentages and costs and everything.
Do you have a formal signing on document that we can share with the board Monday?
Yeah, so we have an engagement letter which covers all of that, which I can send out straight after this call.
And so the process after that would be engagement letter signed.
Then we have a kickoff call which is the deep dive with my team.
So the deal team that will be going out and marketing in the first instance, they go through a bunch of questions to make sure that we get everything right in the marketing materials and the listing.
And also they are pitching the deal to potential buyers.
So they need to kind of understand what it is as well so they can explain it and get excited about it.
And then once we've got that, it takes about two or three weeks to get everything together, get the listing up and then go market.
And then another week or so for replies to come back through.
We're probably looking at a four week setup before we would expect to start putting meetings into your calendar.
Two weeks press, two week reply and then after a month we have an idea of what the interest is.
Yeah, yeah, exactly.
Yeah, yeah.
If there's, I mean if it's completely straightforward and there's no issues, we should be flying by week five, six and meetings being booked in from then on in.
So you probably have about two or three months of meetings to look forward at least.
What's your advice on where we put.
When we're thinking about ebitda, where we put salaries, we expect to pull out.
So director salaries in particular, if I was doing say a 12 month earn out, do you consider it with a director salary in, do you try and apportion some of that?
What would you expect us to be doing?
Yeah, so I mean on a 60% margin, I don't know what is included in there, but it may be that you're being paid out of dividends.
So we would look at a market rate salary to adjust that for whoever was going to be in the business.
Yeah, it's not, it's not done through dividends.
It's done in as a, as a.
Standard salary, which is great because then then the argument is that it is a 6.
It's a true 60% margin, so.
Correct.
So the 60% margin is excluding effectively the overhead costs, support costs.
So I think the buyer, if we went to market at 60%, the buyer may, we've got to be careful not to make them really skeptical of your numbers.
So there is a sort of balancing act to get right.

Obviously it's great 60% but if that does exclude huge amount of costs which can be factored in once the holding company has moved out of the equation, then the buyer is just going to put all of those back and they will put in their own expectations of what those costings are.
So it might be better to kind of assume what all of your costs are and put them in to, you know, the overhead and reduce the margin to something that's more realistic.
So that'd be good to have to have that really.
It's about getting your story as straight as possible and not creating too much friction in the, in the process once we get a buyer.
So will we be preparing the declared accounts and then looking at normalized accounts so what they would look like after.
Yeah, I mean we can do that as part of the process, the valuation process and preparing you to go to market.
So we would look at that.

But obviously if you guys have an idea of what it is, I mean it probably is straightforward for you la to say there's this, this and this and we would say, you know, dial that back by 100k and then we would just, yeah, we would include that in the financials as part of the overhead and it would be great to have it all prepared because they will then just start throwing numbers at us that they want it to be adjusted down by.
So yeah, preparation is key really.
Okay, so I think timing wise, yeah, Monday is.
So we'll have a.
If you can share that document that you mentioned after this meeting then we'll share that with the board so they can have a read through beforehand.
I think we're clear.

Two weeks to do the prep, two weeks to get replies and then two weeks after that start getting meetings in place, looking about 4 to 6 EBITDA valuation until we get a competitive tension bidding war going on and then sky's the limit.
Yeah.
And then the earnout.
I think we need to be clear just to make it clear.
So Chris is moving, would be moving his time to the software business but will still be available and to make sure there's a smooth transition.

And the story is that as a business we're moving the focus into the software business and that's why we're looking to the best of it so the team can concentrate on software business rather than services business.
Yeah.
So what I would advise, Brian is with the, with the forecast for the Year, you know, after it's bought is to kind of, I mean, you want it to be a little bit sexy.
You don't want to be too, you know, too flat on that.
But just have something realistic and really doable, something that will get them excited, but something that you know you can smash is, is kind of the best deal.
We actually call it sandbagging in M and A.
So you kind of set their expectations lower than what you know you can deliver and then smash out a part.
Yeah, that's the deal.
And then like I said, with our client in Austin, they were able to actually leave three months early.
We've done that in a recent deal as well where we can see that our clients going to smash it.
They actually have a two year gap for the next payout.
But their forecasts were really, really good and based on them knowing that they could absolutely smash them, which they're already doing.
So that would be my advice, is come to the party with something that looks like that.
Strong and stable business.
It's not a high growth, it's a good, stable business that generates good cash.
Not stratospheric.
You know, this is a good landing pad for a US company that wants to set up a UK base.
But how many people are in the team?
Sorry, Brian.
Nine.
Yeah.
Which is good.
Yeah.
For setting up in the UK.
That's a nice stable team.
Usually sort of around 12.
They look for just over 10, but I think 9 is probably okay.
A couple of new hires.
Okay, cool.
Yeah, all totally doable, I think, just as long as you get the story straight at the start and then we don't face a barrage of questions.
Just give them the answers before they, they add the question.
Anymore.
Anymore.
Any other questions?
All good for me.
You're good?
No, all good, thank you.
Okay, cool.
Well, let's, yeah, let's get to the next stage.
We'll wait for that document.
We'll come back to you Monday afternoon.
All going well and yeah, take it from there.
Okay, perfect.
All right, brilliant.
Good to see you all again.
Good to see you again, Brian.
Good to see you guys.
I'll get that to you as soon as possible.
Thanks, Andy.
Cheers.
All right, cheers.
But.

summary.overview: The Capital A meeting focused on the strategic aspects of business development and mergers and acquisitions, featuring participants Andrew Day, Brian Fitzpatrick, Chris Liversidge, and Lee-Anne Lindsay. The session began with light conversation and a review of current market trends in acquisitions, including concerns about external factors like Trump's trade war. Capital A, an M&A advisory specializing in marketing services, outlined its three-tier service approach, with an emphasis on transparency and ongoing support throughout the M&A process. The discussion included critical topics like EBITDA valuation, the importance of market tension, and confidentiality measures for agency listings. Next steps were clarified, including the preparation of an engagement letter for board approval and logistics for upcoming meetings. Action items were assigned, focusing on financial presentations and account normalization preparations ahead of the formal engagements.
summary.short_summary: The Capital A meeting emphasized strategic business development and mergers and acquisitions, featuring participants Andrew Day, Brian Fitzpatrick, Chris Liversidge, and Lee-Anne Lindsay. The session began with light conversation and an overview of current market trends in acquisitions, particularly concerns regarding external factors like Trump's trade war. Capital A, an M&A advisory firm specializing in marketing services, presented its three-tier service approach, which includes a free listing on Agencies Co, valuation preparation for $5,000, and a comprehensive six-month process with a tailored buyer list. Key topics included the importance of EBITDA valuation, the role of market tension, and confidentiality measures for agency listings. Next steps involved preparing an engagement letter for board approval and organizing logistics for upcoming meetings, with specific action items assigned to ensure thorough financial presentations and account normalization.
